Adult chilipepper rockfish (Sebastes goodei) commonly attain a maximum total length of 56 centimeters [Li = 56 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger-bodied species in the genus Sebastes. This ultimate length is typically achieved after several decades of slow growth, a life-history pattern common to many long-lived rockfishes inhabiting the continental slope of the eastern North Pacific. In contrast, the onset of reproductive maturity occurs at a substantially smaller size, with puberty being reached at a total length of 32 centimeters [Lp = 32 centimeters]. This marked disparity between length at maturity and ultimate length suggests an extended adult phase during which females can allocate considerable resources to annual reproductive bouts. Field studies off central California have consistently documented that females become reproductively active only after several years of somatic growth, a delay that likely reflects the energetic demands of producing large broods of live young. The length-at-maturity estimates were derived from macroscopic examination of gonads collected during bottom trawl surveys conducted by the National Marine Fisheries Service.

At parturition, the larval offspring of chilipepper rockfish emerge at an exceedingly small size, with each newly extruded larva having a wet weight of only 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams]. This remarkably low birth mass is a direct consequence of the species' reproductive strategy as a viviparous rockfish, in which females give birth to thousands of tiny, free-swimming larvae rather than large, well-provisioned offspring. The yolk reserves of each larva are contained within an egg that measures approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter prior to internal fertilization and subsequent development within the ovarian cavity. Such a diminutive starting mass underscores a high-risk early life stage, where larvae must immediately begin exogenous feeding in the plankton to avoid starvation. Mortality during this pelagic period is thought to be extremely high, a common feature of marine teleosts that produce small offspring in large numbers. The energetic investment per larva is minimal, but the cumulative reproductive output of a single mature female can be substantial.

Fully grown adult chilipepper rockfish attain a maximum wet weight of approximately 2,500 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,500 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to the species. This ultimate body mass, reached only after many years of steady growth, contrasts sharply with the mass at which females first become capable of reproduction. Individuals at the onset of puberty typically weigh around 447.6 grams [Wwp = around 447.6 grams], a threshold that represents only a fraction of the maximum adult mass. The nearly sixfold difference between weight at maturity and ultimate weight indicates a prolonged period of adult growth during which females can increase their body size substantially, thereby enhancing their fecundity with each successive spawning season. Field observations from the Southern California Bight suggest that most females will have surpassed this pubertal weight by the time they are several years old, though individual growth rates vary with local prey availability and thermal history.

The annual reproductive output of female chilipepper rockfish is remarkably high; to offset the extremely high larval mortality rates typical of pelagic marine teleosts, individuals produce approximately 2,740 larvae per day [Ri = approximately 2,740 larvae per day] when maintained at a stable bottom temperature of 8.2 °C [T = 8.2 °C], with the largest females contributing disproportionately to the annual larval pool. This per-day estimate corresponds to over one million larvae per female per year, a value that aligns with the reproductive output documented for related Sebastes species. The maximum reproductive rate is achieved only by the largest and oldest females, whose greater body cavity volume allows for the development of more advanced embryos during the extended gestation period characteristic of viviparous rockfishes. In the cool, stable thermal environment of the continental slope, where water temperatures rarely deviate from this 8.2 °C [T = 8.2 °C] baseline, the long gestation period ensures that larvae are released during the spring plankton bloom, maximizing their chances of encountering suitable prey. Variations in fecundity among individuals are primarily driven by differences in female size and age.

The maximum lifespan of chilipepper rockfish is considerable, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of approximately 12,775 days [am = approximately 12,775 days] when residing in waters at 8.2 °C [T = 8.2 °C]. This longevity is characteristic of many rockfish species and is closely linked to the stable, cold temperatures found on the outer continental shelf and upper slope, where metabolic demands are relatively low. Under such thermal conditions, the species exhibits a slow pace of life, with delayed maturity, slow somatic growth, and extended reproductive life spans. The ability to survive for multiple decades allows females to accumulate numerous spawning events across their lifetime, a key demographic feature that buffers the population against occasional years of poor larval survival. Comparisons with sympatric Sebastes species indicate that chilipepper rockfish have an intermediate life span, shorter than the most extreme examples like Sebastes aleutianus but longer than many shallower-dwelling congeners. This longevity is a critical consideration for fisheries management, as the species is particularly vulnerable to overexploitation.
